title.narrative: Pillar 2: Enable a more accountable, evidence-based and inclusive response in the delivery of mental health services and data collection in underserved areas for Embrace.

description.narrative:
ltpgtltspan style="font-family:"gtThe National Lifeline in Lebanon provides emotional support and suicide prevention, but in recent years, it has also played a significant role in coordinated response and increasing information on accountability and inclusion in humanitarian activities. The current situation in Lebanon has worsened the impact of social and economic factors on mental health. In 2022, the Lifeline received 12,481 calls, a 1.3-fold increase from the previous year, indicating a greater need for its services. Around 18% of these calls involved individuals seeking referrals for humanitarian services, which can act as a risk factor for mental wellbeing. The Lifeline serves as a main source of orientation for beneficiaries accessing mental health and non-mental health services, including protection, livelihood, and cash assistance. With funding from LHF in 2022, the Lifeline launched more focused social work activities and a dedicated MEAL officer to improve the quality of humanitarian response. Data analysis shows that the National Lifeline successfully orients 57% of calls requesting referral information, with 69% being referred to non-profit organizations. However, some community needs, such as shelters for specific populations, remain limited or unavailable, decreasing successful referral rates. Moreover, only 39% of the referrals granted are accessed, with challenges like the service not responding, the service not following- up with the beneficiary, an inconvenience in the location of the service, a long waiting list or the service ceasing its activities. These findings provide valuable evidence to strengthen inclusion and accountability in the humanitarian sector and guide future investments. lt/spangtltbrgtlt/pgtltpgt
lt/pgtltp style="mso-margin-top-alt:automso-margin-bottom-alt:auto" class="MsoNormal"gtltspan style="font-size:10.5ptfont-family:" lang="EN-US"gtThe increase in calls to the Lifeline also reflects an increase in callers identifying stressors, major life events, and mental distress as risk factors for their mental health. Callers are increasingly requesting referrals to specialized mental health services, even when the primary need is for non-mental health services. Dissatisfaction among callers with low-rated satisfaction is linked to limited access to specialized mental health services due to resource constraints. These limitations, including lack of phone credit and transportation costs, decrease the capacity to build sustainable mental health systems across Lebanon. Therefore, projects are needed to strengthen access and coordination among existing localized services. lt/spangtlt/pgtltpgt
lt/pgtltp style="mso-margin-top-alt:automso-margin-bottom-alt:auto" class="MsoNormal"gtltspan style="font-size:10.5ptfont-family:" lang="EN-US"gtWhile localized mental health services are available within identified networks of Primary Health Care Centers PHCCs under the National Mental Health Program, local communities find diverse challenges to accessing them. From follow up calls with Lifeline beneficiaries, these challenges are beginning to become more apparent to actors in the field for respective response plans. Low mental health literacy is apparent and particularly in remote areas where a limited understanding of mental illness, symptoms, the role of mental health professionals and beliefs of treatment negatively impact local communities’ intentions to seek mental health services. Furthermore, false perceptions of waiting time, availability of services and professionals and the cost of care are all evidence-based factors found to decrease a sense of capacity to continue care which in turn results in reluctance to access care to begin with. Based on these field findings, Embrace has mobilized awareness and outreach efforts and a clinical professional to remote areas with limited mental health literacy and proximity to PHCCs with mental health services. Awareness sessions, psychiatric assessments, and orientation to longer-term care within a 20-minute travel parameter will be offered to diverse communities across Lebanon. This project’s activities are tracked with monitoring and evaluation follow- up calls to collect feedback on experiencing and quality of services increasing accountability and inclusion from vulnerable populations. lt/spangtlt/pgtltpgt
